How about

"If maintainers enable checks beyond these, they shall ensure that within 5 business days of a new clang release, all tidy errors in the new checks have been resolved."

Honestly, the tidy updates themselves have been getting easier in the last few years, clang compiler warnings have been the issue.   I would much rather that we have some experience with the checks before we try to enable them project wide.  There's a lot of checks in the next patch that we know cause problems that we don't have solutions to;  I'd rather there be a path for checks to be enabled selectively on a per repo basis ahead of doing it in docs.

Shouldn't we be able to put them in the "future options" section then if a maintainer wants to enable them?

The purpose of having them in a central place is that we can then encourage discussion before people turn on checks that aren't appropriate.  That was the biggest hang up with when Jayanth tried to enable everything to me is it was seeming to be an assorted set of things.

> Shouldn't we be able to put them in the "future options" section then if a maintainer wants to enable them?
> 
> The purpose of having them in a central place is that we can then encourage discussion before people turn on checks that aren't appropriate.  That was the biggest hang up with when Jayanth tried to enable everything to me is it was seeming to be an assorted set of things.

What if we change to "If maintainers want to enable a new check, they should first open a review to add it to this list to begin a discussion".  I don't want a docs MERGE to be a requirement, but sure, opening a review is reasonable.

If we had this rule previously, https://gerrit.openbmc.org/c/openbmc/docs/+/82879 would still be stalled waiting on the feedback of a non-maintainer to render an opinion, and that check wouldn't be available.

I don't want a case where there's a check a maintainer thinks is useful for their repository, and is easy to enable, but they're prevented from doing so because of the lack of merge here.

Personally when I get time to work on tidy checks, it's 20 minutes in between meetings to go fix the bugs and enable a check.  In general my workflow is to enable every tidy check, and see which ones are accomplishable in a short timeframe. The more friction we add in waiting on merges for this desired list, the fewer checks I can enable in that 20 minutes I have.

If there are checks that we KNOW are harmful and should never enable absolutely, lets get those written down to give guard rails (and you've already done the start of that).

I'm not sure how to reconcile your suggestion with the next sentence and the goals here.  You wrote:

> What if we change to "If maintainers want to enable a new check, they should first open a review to add it to this list to begin a discussion". I don't want a docs MERGE to be a requirement, but sure, opening a review is reasonable.

To me that means someone can just propose a change here and merge it in their repo (without any feedback).  I don't really know how that solves anything.

The next sentence states:

> If a new `clang-tidy` check is useful, a change to the reference is sufficient and should not have much friction.

That's the goal: low friction for new changes.  I don't think 82879 is a good example because if we were driving to consensus well on the dependent commit, I think we'd just power through the unresponsive feedback (or at least the proposer could ask that we just move forward and I think we should honor that).

I do think it is reasonable:
  1. make a fix/enable change in one or more repos and push a pending commit to Gerrit to show viability
  2. make the proposal here
  3. merge (1) once (2) has consensus.

A later commit here "catches" us up to clang-21.  I guess we could make a prereq for a new clang version that we go through and make a disposition on each new clang-tidy warning... do we want to do that?

> I'm not sure how to reconcile your suggestion with the next sentence and the goals here.

Probably because there is a fundamental disagreement with the stated goals.

>  I don't want a docs MERGE to be a requirement, but sure, opening a review is reasonable.

I have this same concern/desire.  I prefer consistency not be an impediment to forward progress.

> To me that means someone can just propose a change here and merge it in their repo (without any feedback). I don't really know how that solves anything.

Yes.  They are maintainers of that piece of code, we already trust them to not do things that impact that code outside of the actual checks enabled.  Adding a new check is significantly less trust than we already put in them.

Paraphrasing what's here diffferently: "Any experimentation with a tidy check requires all docs maintainers to agree". I feel like that stalls progress, and I'm ironically proving my own point here by continuing to drag this out.

> If a new clang-tidy check is useful, a change to the reference is sufficient and should not have much friction.

I don't agree with that sentence.  Lot of these checks look good in the first review, but the implementation of them in practice makes the code worse.  readability-function-cognitive-complexity is a great example of something that might be great in theory, but the check itself has scruples (doesn't handle lambdas, complexity isn't well documented, rejects single line patches or reformats) in the implementation that make it really hard to enforce in some repos.

Is there a possible compromise here where both of the following are true:

1 - maintainers are free to merge and experiment with checks before they go into the reference
2 - anyone doing toolchain upgrades (or any other activity where tidy checks have been hindersome) has license to remove non-sanctioned checks when they get in the way?

I'm fine with Brads suggestion above, and in absence of these rules, that's what's happening anyway.  Every new version of clang that comes out, I generally will be working the new compiler version ahead of the release.

For example,  bmcweb had to disable include-cleaner for a while because of some really bad behavior it had in combination with dependencies.
https://github.com/openbmc/bmcweb/commit/2ca561945f9c518e4916cd23c194f89816fdbeee

FWIW, this same thing happens with compiler warnings:
https://github.com/openbmc/bmcweb/blob/430b30bd5f800b5c7dc0b2bd856f71f72b93c785/meson.build#L106
Ok, I think we're on the same page with this statement, I just think it's in conflict with the last comment.
I made a minor edit here.  What I'm suggesting is that someone makes proposed changes to multiple repositories to show the change is viable, then we approve the change here.
Having this list will be great.  I'll add the things I know.
